summary: Carbonear Island Light, lit in 1878 at the mouth of Carbonear harbour: a 1697 refuge, kept by the Forwards from 1882 to 1928, automated after that.

lens.note: Order given in the 1879 almanac, as quoted by LighthouseFriends

structures.type: wood tower and dwelling in one building
structures.note: Standing at least until 1955 (LighthouseFriends); a 2010 photograph shows foundation ruins (Lighthouse Directory)
Rectangular skeleton tower, red and white daymark (Canadian Coast Guard list)

staffing.note: Automated after Henry G. Forward died in 1928; LighthouseFriends gives no year for the change

events.note: Residents of Carbonear took refuge on the island and defended it against French raiders (plaque text as reproduced by LighthouseFriends)
Island defended again by local people led by William Pynne against a French force from Placentia (plaque text)
Placed in operation in 1878 with George Taylor as keeper
Small store built at the landing place; keeper given winter sashes for the dwelling
Henry F. Forward appointed after Keeper Taylor died on the island in 1882
Automated after Henry G. Forward's death; characteristic changed from fixed white to a white flash every five seconds
Island's 1697 and 1705 history designated a national historic event

corrections.proposed: original wood tower and dwelling: lost (foundation ruins by 2010); current rectangular skeleton tower, 4.3 m, standing
corrections.why: The record treats the 1878 wood structure as standing. LighthouseFriends says it was standing until at least 1955; the Lighthouse Directory shows only foundation ruins in a 2010 photograph. The Canadian Coast Guard list gives the current skeleton tower as 4.3 m.
The record's agency is null. The Canadian Coast Guard publishes the List of Lights entry used for the current characteristic. Human check of ownership still needed.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: OpenStreetMap maps a standing structure because it shows the current skeleton tower. The original wood tower and dwelling are gone: LighthouseFriends says standing until at least 1955, and the Lighthouse Directory shows foundation ruins in a 2010 photograph.

The Wikidata coordinates (47 44 24 N, 53 09 22 W) repeat the position printed in the 1879 almanac, as LighthouseFriends quotes it. The Canadian Coast Guard list gives 47 44 22.6 N, 053 09 51.7 W, which matches OpenStreetMap. The difference is about 618 m, from the almanac's rounding and the older position.

notes_for_editor: Designation date: LighthouseFriends gives 1954 for a national historic event. Wikipedia gives 1954 for a site of national significance and 1981 for a nationally historic event; not cited. The Parks Canada Directory of Federal Heritage Designations (page id 1055, read through WebFetch, not the cache) gives designation date 1954-06-07 and the plaque text. The cached copy has no designation text, so it is not cited. A human should check whether a 1981 designation exists. Focal height: the 1879 almanac gives 195 feet above sea level (about 59 m); the Canadian Coast Guard list gives 54.3 m above water and the Lighthouse Directory 54 m (177 ft). Wikipedia and Wikidata give 195 m, which appears to repeat the almanac's feet figure as metres; not cited, left unresolved. Keepers: names and years are LighthouseFriends' (its text gives George Taylor and George H. Taylor, and a keeper line with dates; the dashes in that line are not reliable). No USLHS roster (Canada), and the Canadian Department of Marine reports in the corpus hold no hit for Carbonear (Newfoundland was not in the Dominion until 1949). Newspapers: none searched, as Chronicling America does not hold St. John's papers. Not checked: the Journal of the House of Assembly of Newfoundland, which LighthouseFriends cites for petitions and grants, and the Encyclopedia of Newfoundland and Labrador. The 1928 obituary is cited as LighthouseFriends quotes it. The 'after the keepers' material is in Today because the sourced material is short. Story is a thin-shape piece with no headings. Fact-check 2026-10-28: the body runs to about 500 words with no headings, which sits at the bottom of the moderate length band (2 to 4 chapters) rather than the thin band (150 to 400 words); the editor should choose between adding chapters and trimming. The 1879 almanac's visibility (16 miles) and the list's nominal range (7 nm) are different measures and are not compared in the story.
